name: Sociedade Vegetariana Brasileira: institutional meat reduction (Segunda Sem Carne), 2023
summary: Sociedade Vegetariana Brasileira (SVB) runs Segunda Sem Carne (Meatless Monday) in Brazil, getting schools, popular restaurants, social-assistance centres and hospitals to serve plant-based meals at least one day a week; this models that institutional work in 2023, the latest year with published accounts: about 45 million meals that year from menu changes won over about fifteen years, paid for by about a quarter of SVB's programme spending, whose fifteen years of wins are set against fifteen years of spending. It comes to about 11 years of healthy life per $1,000. Each won menu change counts the site's years a won reform counts, and the estimate is a past average (wins over spending), so it takes the next-dollar factor, unlike most diet-change models. The result is mostly uncertainty: how much a fish's suffering counts, the suffering in a replaced meal, the share of spending on this programme and SVB's own unverified meal counts; SVB's certification, events, courses and content (about three-quarters of its spending) are not valued, for want of any reach or spending data.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for every animal model. The shared SAD figures are Ambitious Impact's, which count each species' pain as a share of a person's with its own species weights. Here those weights come out and Rethink Priorities' go in, so every species is counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain. How a chicken compares with a person is the one animal slider.

rows.label: Share of programme spending on institutional meat reduction and municipal menu work
rows.explainer: SVB's accounts don't split costs by programme, so the share is our judgment, anchored on headcount (Convention 1). Of about 38 working staff on SVB's team page (2026, the only year published), six to eight work on institutional meals and the municipal menu bills: food programmes and policies (3), institutional programmes and partnerships (1), government relations (1), gastronomy, which trains institutional cooks (1), and the nutrition department's project coordinator (1): 15–21%. With a share of leadership and communications, 25%. Low end 15% (the narrow team only); high end 40% (if the nutrition department's training of health professionals and much of communications serve the institutional programme). The rest pays for the Selo Vegano certification, VegFest and events, the volunteer network, health-professional courses and content, which this model doesn't value. The share is applied to every year of the campaign; in 2015–2018 events (VegFest) took a larger share of spending (52% in 2015, 'Despesas com Eventos 381.399,18'), which would lower the institutional share in those years; the low end allows for it.

rows.explainer: SVB's campaign manager's count at the campaign's tenth anniversary (October 2019): meals served without meat in partner schools, popular restaurants, social-assistance centres, hospitals and companies. A count SVB compiles from its partners; it publishes no method. The page carries no date; October 2019 is from its image path (/2019/10/) and the tenth anniversary it marks. It counts meals 'oferecidas' (offered), the 2024 count meals 'servidas' (served) with plant protein: probably the same tally worded differently, but the difference is one reason for the delivery adjustment.

rows.explainer: The tenth anniversary (2019) and the fifteenth (2024): five years between the two cumulative counts.

rows.label: Meals served in 2023 relative to the yearly average of October 2019 to October 2024
rows.explainer: SVB publishes no count for 2023. The five-year average (40.6 million a year, October 2019 to October 2024) includes 2020 and 2021, when Brazilian schools, the largest partners, were closed for long periods, so 2023 was probably somewhat above it: 1.1. Anchors: about 47 million meals in the public network in 2017 (pt.wikipedia, https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Vegetariana_Brasileira, citing Folha de S.Paulo, April 2018), 67 million in 2018 (SVB, https://svb.org.br/2501-segunda-sem-carne-atinge-marca-de-67-milhoes-de-refeicoes-em-2018/) and 81 million in 2019 (a 2022 thesis citing SVB, https://axis.ghc.com.br/bitstreams/b8125e84-7f9a-4ed9-8b20-3da5a5b331b3/download), 2.0 times the five-year average. If 2023 had returned to the 2019 level, the other four years would average only about 30 million, below the 2017 level even with the closures, so a full return is unlikely. Low 0.8 (partners lost after the pandemic); high 1.6 (most of the way back to 2019). SVB's running totals aren't fully consistent (a 2021 article gives 'more than 300 million'), which is part of the delivery adjustment.

rows.explainer: The year's whole flow from all of SVB's institutional partners, old and new (schools, popular restaurants, social-assistance centres, hospitals, companies): about 45 million meals. SVB's own count, not independently verified; delivery shortfalls are in the delivery adjustment, and whether each meal replaces an animal-product meal in the evidence adjustment.

rows.explainer: SVB's yearly count for 2019, the pre-pandemic peak, as cited in a 2022 thesis (SVB's own pages give about 80 million).

rows.label: Share of the fall from 2019 to 2023 that is partnerships lapsed (rather than counting or recovery)
rows.explainer: The yearly count fell from 81 million meals in 2019 to about 45 million in 2023. Some of that is partners that stopped, wins that ran and lapsed; some is how SVB counts and meals still recovering after the pandemic. Half, our judgment, from none to all.

rows.label: Yearly meals of menu changes won since 2009 that had lapsed by 2023
rows.explainer: Menu changes SVB won that ran for a while and then stopped were wins too, and count their years like the rest: the share of the 2019-to-2023 fall that is lapsed partnerships, in meals a year (about 18 million).

rows.label: Meals per year added by the menu changes SVB wins in a year (average of 2009–2023)
rows.explainer: Everything SVB won in fifteen years, in meals a year (the changes still running in 2023 plus those that lapsed), spread over the fifteen years: about 4 million meals a year added per year of SVB's work. Each won change then counts the site's years a won reform counts (below), not for as long as it runs, so old wins aren't credited again every year (docs/normalization.md 2.9). The cost below is the average yearly spending over the same fifteen years.

rows.label: SADs averted per meal replaced
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for a replaced meal (Sinergia's Latin American canteen meal, 2024 SADs) times the meal-mix ratio below. Never rebuilt from a meat mix of your own.

rows.label: Suffering in a replaced meal here, relative to the reference meal
rows.explainer: 1: the shared per-meal figure is Sinergia Animal's Latin American canteen meal, and SVB's meals are Brazilian school, popular-restaurant and canteen meals, the same kind of meal in the same region (docs/normalization.md 2.9). The range is the template's half to double: no published comparison of Brazilian institutional meals with the reference meal was found, and menus rotating beef, chicken, fish and eggs could move the mix either way.

rows.label: Fall in production per meal not eaten
rows.explainer: Fewer meals bought lowers production by less than one for one, because prices fall and others buy more (Norwood and Lusk 2011).

rows.label: Years a won menu change counts
rows.explainer: A menu change SVB wins counts the site's one number of years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway (docs/normalization.md 2.9; 5 by default), discounted at the shared rate; meal policies take effect at once, so there is no wait.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Whether a meal served without meat replaces an animal-product meal in what people eat, one for one. Two parts. (1) The meals are 'proteína vegetal' meals, vegetarian rather than vegan: some carry eggs or dairy, so part of the animal product stays: 0.85 (0.7–0.95). (2) Compensation and skipping: diners may eat more meat at other meals, or skip the plant-based meal; Garnett et al. (2019, PNAS) found no detectable rebound at other mealtimes when a university's cafeterias served more vegetarian meals, but school pupils on a fixed menu can't switch and may eat more at home: 0.85 (0.65–0.95). Product 0.72; ends 0.45 and 0.9. Anchor: the template's 0.7 for institutional meal change.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The share of the meals in the counted years that wouldn't have been served without SVB. How long a change would have taken to come anyway is already in the years a won reform counts, so this asks only whether, within those years, the institution would have gone meat-free one day a week without SVB: through Brazil's school-meal guidelines, other groups' programmes (Humane Society International's Alimentação Consciente Brasil, Sinergia Animal) or its own nutritionists. SVB brought the campaign to Brazil and set up the large partnerships itself: 0.85 (0.6–0.95), our judgment.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: SVB's share of the resources behind the meals. City and state education and social-assistance departments design and cook the menus (their nutritionists, CODAE in São Paulo, the cooks SVB trains), and other groups help in some places (Humane Society International took part in São Paulo's prison menus). The food itself costs no more, so it isn't a contribution to the change; the partners' staff time is. Our judgment: 0.6 (0.35–0.9). Co-funders' resources lower this share and never enter the cost (Convention 2).

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: The share of the meals SVB counts that were actually served meat-free as planned. SVB's count is compiled from partners' figures and published only as rounded running totals, with no method; schools change menus, pupils are absent, and some partners stop without telling. 0.8 (0.6–0.95), our judgment; the template's default, widened downward because the count is the charity's own.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: Your value, shared with every model built on an organisation's past average (Your values: "How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far"). This estimate is a past average: the menu changes SVB won over fifteen years (2009–2023), set against its average yearly spending over the same years, not items more money buys again at a known price. The next dollar goes to new partners, which are harder to win than São Paulo's schools were. 50% by default (our judgment), from 18% to 100%.
